summary: South of Market is where the city has always put the work. The first permits after the fire are for engines and boilers in workshops — two of them at 553 Brannan Street for a planing mill — and for stables: forty horses for Jones & McGill off Folsom Street in 1907, twenty-two for the New French Baking Company on Tehama Street in 1913, twelve for Blumenau & Neuman on Natoma Street in 1914. The Board did not just say yes. In March 1916 it refused R. O'Banion a stable at 1237 Folsom Street, took the application up again in May, and granted him a stable "for 12 horses only" — he had asked for thirty. Four years earlier a neighbour, Mrs. Hannah Banker, had come and stood before the Board to argue against a stable on Stillman Street. Laundries were licensed the same careful way, with the power written into the permit: hand or electric only for Paul Verdier at 310 Seventh Street in 1908, an engine and boiler for the Galland Mercantile Laundry on Eighth Street, eight horsepower for a rescue mission's laundry at 884 Folsom Street, and a five-thousand-gallon oil tank behind the Bay City Steam Laundry at 910 Folsom Street. When the Board started dividing the kerb doorway by doorway around 1930, the names it wrote down here were makers and warehouses, not banks: forty-five feet at 485 Brannan Street for Liggett & Myers Tobacco, eighteen at 1093 Mission Street for the Chicago Artificial Limb Company, eighteen at 1464 Howard Street for the Stella Metal Casket Company. Then the city moved its own difficult business in. The building that went up in the block between Seventh, Bryant, Harrison and Harriet was given to the successor firm of the architects who designed City Hall, and in 1957 a new street was cut between Sixth and Harriet to serve the new Hall of Justice; from there the record is lease after lease — six floors and half a basement on Jessie Street, a public health clinic at 250 Fourth Street, the Public Defender's offices on Boardman Place. The workshops became flats twice over: bonds in 1985 to buy and repair the empty Hueblein Building at 601 Fourth Street, then a run of live-work conversions around 2000 — The Lofts at 712 Bryant Street, 950 Harrison Street, 1150 Folsom Street. The end of that boom is in the record too. In December 2000 the Board asked whether the space "newly vacated by the closing of Pets.com at 435 Brannan Street" might be taken for courtrooms. It still licenses the district drink by drink, down to a music venue's licence for 1535 Folsom Street in 2024, and it is still housing people here: 459 hotel rooms at 1231 Market Street kept on through 2020, sixteen and a half million dollars of bonds for the Knox residential hotel at 241 Sixth Street, a lease at 1076 Howard Street for the health department.
